subject: Low-Level Design (LLD)
summary: Low-level design is the interview round where 'design a parking lot' means: turn a one-line, deliberately vague prompt into 5-10 small classes with clean responsibilities, then survive the scripted follow-up 'now add X' without rewriting everything. Companies test it because it predicts the thing DSA rounds cannot — whether your code can be merged, extended, and reviewed by a team without regret. The grading is structural: no god classes, is-a vs has-a chosen deliberately, interfaces at the points a requirement says 'for now', and dependencies (clocks, dice, pricing) injected so everything is testable. Study it by drilling the 4-step method (requirements -> entities -> relationships -> code, on a 45-minute budget) and then rehearsing the eight canonical designs in this subject — parking lot, elevator, Splitwise, LRU cache, BookMyShow, notifications, rate limiter, Snake & Ladder — until you can code each core flow with a demo and asserts, and can point, for every design, at the exact seam where the interviewer's probe will land.

sections.title: 1. What an LLD Round Actually Tests
sections.content:
You already know two other interview formats. The DSA round asks: can you make this correct and fast? The HLD round (high-level design: boxes and arrows across many machines — load balancers, databases, queues) asks: can you scale it? The LLD round asks a different question: if I merged your code into my team's codebase, would I regret it in six months?

That is why the prompt is one vague line — "design a parking lot" — and then silence. The vagueness is the first test. The interviewer wants to see whether you extract requirements before writing code, because engineers who code first and ask later ship the wrong thing. The second test comes twenty minutes in, when your design works and they say "now add EV charging spots" or "now support a weekend discount". That probe is scripted in advance. They are checking whether your change is a NEW small class plugged into an existing seam, or a painful edit spread across five old classes.

```
DSA round : one function      -> graded on correctness + complexity
LLD round : 5-10 classes      -> graded on decomposition + extensibility
HLD round : many machines     -> graded on scaling trade-offs
```

Concretely, an LLD interviewer grades four things. One: class decomposition — does each class have one describable job, or did you write a god class (one class that knows everything and does everything, a ParkingLot with 40 methods)? Two: relationship choices — is-a (inheritance) only where a subclass truly is a substitutable variant, has-a (composition) everywhere else. Three: pattern use where it earns its place — a Strategy for pricing is good; a Singleton bolted on to look smart is a negative signal. Four: how you react to change requests. Working code with a god class fails this round. Clean classes with one small bug usually pass, because the bug is a five-minute fix and the structure is the thing being bought.

sections.title: 2. The 4-Step Method and the 45-Minute Budget
sections.content:
A 45-minute LLD round dies in one of two ways: you talk about requirements for 25 minutes and never code, or you start coding at minute 2 and rewrite everything at minute 30 when a requirement you never asked about lands. The 4-step method exists to prevent both. Budget it like this:

```
0        5               15                20                     40      45
|--------|---------------|-----------------|----------------------|-------|
 STEP 1     STEP 2           STEP 3            STEP 4               probes
 clarify    entities:        relationships     code the core        + tests
 require-   nouns->classes   is-a / has-a,     flow end to end
 ments      verbs->methods   interfaces
```

Step 1 (5 min) — requirements. Ask four to six questions and WRITE the answers as bullets where the interviewer can see them. For a parking lot: which vehicle types? multiple floors? how is the fee computed? what happens when full? The written list matters because at minute 25 you will point at it and say "you said hourly pricing, so pricing is a strategy I can swap".

Step 2 (10 min) — entities. Walk your requirement bullets and underline the nouns: vehicle, spot, floor, ticket, payment. Nouns become classes; verbs (park, unpark, calculate fee) become methods ON the class that owns the data the verb touches. Say each class's job in one sentence. If the sentence needs the word "and", split the class.

Step 3 (5 min) — relationships. Decide is-a versus has-a out loud, because inheritance mistakes are the most expensive thing to undo live. Mark the variation points — places where the requirement says "for now" or "initially" (pricing, dispatch policy, split rules) — and put an interface (in Python, an ABC: abstract base class, a class that only declares methods) at each one.

Step 4 (20 min) — code ONE flow end to end: park a car, get a ticket, unpark, pay. Not every getter, not every edge case. A single working flow through real classes beats ten half-classes. Keep the last five minutes for their "now add X" probe — the method exists so that when the probe comes, the seam is already there.

sections.title: 3. Worked Design: Parking Lot
sections.content:
The parking lot is the default LLD question because it packs every skill into one prompt: an inheritance hierarchy (vehicles), a capacity-allocation rule (which spot?), a pluggable policy (pricing), and an obvious god-class trap (put everything in ParkingLot and fail).

Requirements to lock in during step 1:
- Vehicle types: motorcycle, car, truck. A smaller vehicle CAN take a bigger spot; a truck fits only a large spot.
- Multiple floors; a spot belongs to one floor.
- Entry issues a Ticket (which spot, when); exit computes a fee from the ticket.
- Pricing: hourly rate, different per spot size — "for now" (that phrase marks the strategy seam).
- When no spot fits, parking is refused — not queued (confirm this; queuing changes the design).

```
              ParkingLot
              - floors: [ParkingFloor]
              - pricing: PricingStrategy   <- injected
              - active: {plate: Ticket}
              + park(vehicle, hour) -> Ticket | None
              + unpark(plate, hour) -> fee
                |  has-a           |  uses
                v                  v
        ParkingFloor         PricingStrategy (ABC)
        + find_spot(v)             ^ implements
                | has-a       HourlyPricing
                v             (rate per SpotSize)
        ParkingSpot
        - size: SpotSize
        - vehicle | None          Vehicle (ABC, size)
        + can_fit(v)                ^        ^      ^
                              Motorcycle   Car   Truck
```

Three decisions carry the interview. First, spot allocation is BEST FIT — the smallest free spot that fits — and it lives in ParkingFloor.find_spot, not in ParkingLot. Why best fit: with one compact and one large spot free, first-fit would happily put a car in the large spot, and the next truck is refused even though capacity existed. Second, the fee is computed from the SPOT size, not the vehicle: a car that occupied a large spot blocked large capacity and pays the large rate — say this rule out loud, it shows you think about what the price is FOR. Third, ParkingLot holds a PricingStrategy it was given, never builds one; when the probe "add weekend pricing" arrives, you write one new class and change zero existing ones.

The probes to expect: "add EV charging spots" (new SpotSize plus a Chargeable capability — discuss whether charging is a spot property or a new subclass), "nearest spot to entrance" (find_spot gains a distance tiebreak — one method changes), and "multiple entry gates issuing tickets concurrently" (a race condition — two threads touching the same free spot where the result depends on who gets there first — so spot assignment needs a lock or an atomic claim).
sections.code:
"""Parking Lot -- small classes, one job each.
Vehicle knows its size. Spot knows what fits. Floor finds spots.
PricingStrategy computes fees. ParkingLot only coordinates.
"""
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from enum import Enum


class SpotSize(Enum):
    MOTORCYCLE = 1
    COMPACT = 2
    LARGE = 3


class Vehicle(ABC):
    """Base vehicle. Each subclass declares the smallest spot size it fits."""
    size: SpotSize

    def __init__(self, plate: str):
        self.plate = plate


class Motorcycle(Vehicle):
    size = SpotSize.MOTORCYCLE


class Car(Vehicle):
    size = SpotSize.COMPACT


class Truck(Vehicle):
    size = SpotSize.LARGE


class ParkingSpot:
    def __init__(self, spot_id: str, size: SpotSize):
        self.spot_id = spot_id
        self.size = size
        self.vehicle = None          # None means free

    def can_fit(self, vehicle: Vehicle) -> bool:
        return self.vehicle is None and vehicle.size.value <= self.size.value

    def park(self, vehicle: Vehicle) -> None:
        assert self.can_fit(vehicle)
        self.vehicle = vehicle

    def unpark(self) -> None:
        self.vehicle = None


class ParkingFloor:
    def __init__(self, floor_id: int, spots):
        self.floor_id = floor_id
        self.spots = list(spots)

    def find_spot(self, vehicle: Vehicle):
        """Best fit: the SMALLEST free spot that fits, so a car never wastes
        the LARGE spot the next truck will need."""
        candidates = [s for s in self.spots if s.can_fit(vehicle)]
        return min(candidates, key=lambda s: s.size.value) if candidates else None


class Ticket:
    def __init__(self, ticket_id: int, vehicle: Vehicle,
                 spot: ParkingSpot, entry_hour: int):
        self.ticket_id = ticket_id
        self.vehicle = vehicle
        self.spot = spot
        self.entry_hour = entry_hour


class PricingStrategy(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def fee(self, ticket: Ticket, exit_hour: int) -> int: ...


class HourlyPricing(PricingStrategy):
    """Rate depends on the SPOT occupied, not the vehicle -- a car parked in a
    LARGE spot pays the LARGE rate because it blocked that capacity."""
    RATES = {SpotSize.MOTORCYCLE: 10, SpotSize.COMPACT: 20, SpotSize.LARGE: 30}

    def fee(self, ticket: Ticket, exit_hour: int) -> int:
        hours = max(1, exit_hour - ticket.entry_hour)
        return hours * self.RATES[ticket.spot.size]


class ParkingLot:
    def __init__(self, floors, pricing: PricingStrategy):
        self.floors = list(floors)
        self.pricing = pricing       # injected: swap pricing without editing this class
        self.active = {}             # plate -> Ticket
        self._next_id = 1

    def park(self, vehicle: Vehicle, entry_hour: int):
        for floor in self.floors:
            spot = floor.find_spot(vehicle)
            if spot:
                spot.park(vehicle)
                ticket = Ticket(self._next_id, vehicle, spot, entry_hour)
                self._next_id += 1
                self.active[vehicle.plate] = ticket
                return ticket
        return None                  # lot has no spot for this vehicle size

    def unpark(self, plate: str, exit_hour: int) -> int:
        ticket = self.active.pop(plate)
        ticket.spot.unpark()
        return self.pricing.fee(ticket, exit_hour)


# ---- demo + self-checks ----------------------------------------------------
floor = ParkingFloor(0, [
    ParkingSpot("F0-M1", SpotSize.MOTORCYCLE),
    ParkingSpot("F0-C1", SpotSize.COMPACT),
    ParkingSpot("F0-C2", SpotSize.COMPACT),
    ParkingSpot("F0-L1", SpotSize.LARGE),
])
lot = ParkingLot([floor], HourlyPricing())

t_truck = lot.park(Truck("TRK-1"), entry_hour=9)
assert t_truck.spot.spot_id == "F0-L1"            # only LARGE fits a truck

t_car = lot.park(Car("CAR-1"), entry_hour=9)
assert t_car.spot.size == SpotSize.COMPACT        # best fit, not LARGE

t_bike = lot.park(Motorcycle("BIK-1"), entry_hour=10)
assert t_bike.spot.spot_id == "F0-M1"

assert lot.park(Car("CAR-2"), 10) is not None     # second compact spot
assert lot.park(Car("CAR-3"), 10) is None         # full: LARGE held by the truck

fee = lot.unpark("TRK-1", exit_hour=12)           # 3 hours * 30 = 90
assert fee == 90
assert lot.park(Car("CAR-3"), 12).spot.spot_id == "F0-L1"  # freed spot reused
print("parking lot OK -- truck paid", fee)

sections.title: 4. Worked Design: Elevator System (State Machine)
sections.content:
The elevator question tests one specific skill: modelling a thing whose behavior depends on what it is currently doing. The trap is a pile of booleans — is_moving, going_up, doors_open — which allows nonsense combinations like is_moving=True, doors_open=True. A state machine (one enum field naming the current mode, plus explicit rules for which mode follows which) makes invalid states unrepresentable: the elevator IS exactly one of IDLE, MOVING_UP, MOVING_DOWN, DOOR_OPEN.

Requirements to lock in:
- N elevators, M floors; hall calls (someone presses a button on a floor) and cabin requests (someone inside picks a floor).
- This implementation dispatches to the NEAREST pending target — easy to reason about, and the code below does exactly what it says. Production elevators instead use the SCAN idea from disk scheduling (keep direction while targets remain ahead), and “upgrade this to SCAN by remembering a direction” is precisely the extensibility probe an interviewer will hand you.
- Doors open for one tick at a target floor.
- Dispatch policy for hall calls: nearest car — "for now" (there is the seam again).

```
  ElevatorController                  State transitions (ALL of them):
  - elevators: [Elevator]             IDLE      --targets?--> MOVING_UP/DOWN
  + call(floor) -> Elevator           MOVING_*  --arrive----> DOOR_OPEN
  + tick()                            DOOR_OPEN --targets?--> MOVING_UP/DOWN
        | has-a                       DOOR_OPEN --none------> IDLE
        v
  Elevator
  - floor, state: State, targets: set[int]
  + request(floor)     + step()   <- the ONLY place state changes
```

The design splits into two classes with a clean boundary. Elevator owns its own physics: step() is called once per tick (one unit of simulated time) and performs exactly one transition — move one floor, or open doors, or settle to idle. Every legal state change lives inside step(), which is what makes the machine auditable: the interviewer can read one method and verify no transition is missing. ElevatorController owns policy: given a hall call, which car answers? Nearest-car today; a real system uses direction-aware cost (a car moving toward you scores better than a nearer car moving away). Because policy is a separate class, upgrading it is a new controller, not surgery on Elevator.

Note the tick-based simulation instead of threads and sleeps. In an interview you cannot debug a thread; a step() you call in a loop gives you a deterministic, assertable elevator. The probes to expect: "add a weight limit" (a new guard on the DOOR_OPEN -> MOVING transition), "add an emergency stop" (a new state — show you extend the enum and the transition table, nothing else), and "prefer elevators already moving toward the caller" (only the controller's cost function changes).

sections.title: 5. Worked Design: Splitwise (Debt Simplification)
sections.content:
Splitwise tests whether you can turn a fuzzy social idea — "we split the dinner" — into exact arithmetic, and whether you know better than to store money in floats (0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in binary floating point; a ledger that drifts by a paisa is a bug report). Store integer paise: Rs 300 is 30000.

Requirements to lock in:
- Users add expenses: who paid, how much, who participates, how it splits.
- Split modes: equal, exact amounts, percentages — an open list. (Open list = Strategy seam.)
- Anyone can ask: who owes whom, overall?
- "Simplify debts": settle the group in as few payments as possible.

```
  Ledger                            SplitStrategy (ABC)
  - net: {User: paise}                  ^            ^
  + add_expense(payer, amount,     EqualSplit    ExactSplit
               users, strategy)    (remainder     (validates
  + simplify()                      paise spread)  shares sum)
      -> [(debtor, creditor, paise)]

  invariant: sum(net.values()) == 0  -- after every expense, forever
```

Two ideas carry this design. First, the ledger stores NET balances, not a list of pairwise IOUs. After every expense, the payer's net goes up by the full amount and each participant's net goes down by their share. The invariant (a condition that must hold at all times) sum(net) == 0 is your correctness check — state it, assert it. Equal split has a classic off-by-one: 100 paise among 3 people is 33.33...; divmod gives base 33 remainder 1, and the first person absorbs the extra paisa, so shares sum EXACTLY to the amount.

Second, simplification is a greedy match: sort debtors most-negative first and creditors most-positive first, then repeatedly have the biggest debtor pay the biggest creditor min(|debt|, credit); one of the two hits zero each round, so n people with nonzero balances settle in at most n-1 transfers. Say the honest caveat before the interviewer does: n-1 is a guarantee, but the true MINIMUM number of transfers is NP-hard (it hides a subset-sum problem — finding subgroups whose balances cancel exactly lets you save a transfer). For a Splitwise group of 5 friends, greedy is what the real product ships.

Probes to expect: "add percentage split" (one new SplitStrategy class, zero edits elsewhere — this is why strategy was the right call), "show per-group balances" (Ledger per group, a Group has-a Ledger), and "make expenses immutable with an audit trail" (append-only Expense log; net balances become a computed view — an event-sourcing idea, name it and move on).

sections.title: 6. Worked Design: LRU Cache as a Class Design
sections.content:
You have met LRU (least recently used — evict the entry untouched for the longest time) as a DSA exercise. The LLD version grades a different thing: not whether you know the trick, but whether you can package it so the pointer surgery is caged inside one class and the cache reads like plain English.

Requirements to lock in:
- get(key) and put(key, value), both O(1) — that constraint forces the data structures, say so.
- Fixed capacity; on overflow evict the least recently used entry.
- Both get and put count as "using" a key; updating an existing key must not evict.

Why two structures: a hashmap alone finds a value in O(1) but cannot tell you which key is oldest without a scan; a list alone keeps order but takes O(n) to find a key. The combination — hashmap from key to node, doubly linked list holding the nodes in recency order — gives O(1) for both questions. Doubly linked specifically because removing a node from the middle needs its predecessor in O(1); a singly linked list would need an O(n) walk to find it.

```
  LRUCache
  - map:   {key: _Node}          O(1) find
  - order: _DoublyLinkedList     O(1) reorder / evict
  + get(key)    + put(key, value)
        | has-a
        v
  _DoublyLinkedList (sentinel head/tail)
  + add_front(n)   + remove(n)   + pop_back()

  head <-> most-recent <-> ... <-> least-recent <-> tail
                                    ^ evict from here
```

The class-design points the interviewer is watching for. One: _DoublyLinkedList is its own class with three verbs — add_front, remove, pop_back — and LRUCache never touches a prev or next pointer. If your cache methods contain pointer surgery, the abstraction leaked. Two: sentinel nodes (permanent dummy head and tail) mean add and remove never special-case an empty list or an end node — mention that this deletes four if-branches and their bugs. Three: get must MOVE the node to the front, not only read it; forgetting the move is the classic bug, and your demo should assert around it.

Probes to expect: "make it LFU" (least frequently used — the eviction decision changes, so introduce an EvictionPolicy abstraction and note that LFU needs frequency buckets to stay O(1)), "add TTL per entry" (store expires_at on the node; check lazily on get — same lazy-expiry idea as seat locks in section 7), and "make it thread-safe" (one lock around get/put first — correct beats clever — then mention sharding the keyspace into several independently locked LRUCache instances if contention is proven).
sections.code:
"""LRU cache = hashmap (find a node in O(1)) + doubly linked list
(move/evict a node in O(1)). The list is its own class -- the cache never
touches prev/next pointers directly. That separation is the design point.
"""


class _Node:
    __slots__ = ("key", "value", "prev", "next")

    def __init__(self, key=None, value=None):
        self.key, self.value = key, value
        self.prev = self.next = None


class _DoublyLinkedList:
    """Sentinel head/tail (permanent dummy end nodes) so add/remove never
    special-case an empty list or the first/last element."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.head, self.tail = _Node(), _Node()
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head

    def add_front(self, node):
        node.prev, node.next = self.head, self.head.next
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node

    def remove(self, node):
        node.prev.next, node.next.prev = node.next, node.prev

    def pop_back(self):
        node = self.tail.prev
        self.remove(node)
        return node


class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        assert capacity > 0
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.map = {}                        # key -> _Node
        self.order = _DoublyLinkedList()     # front = most recently used

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.map:
            return None
        node = self.map[key]
        self.order.remove(node)              # touching a key moves it to front
        self.order.add_front(node)
        return node.value

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.map:                  # update: refresh value + recency
            node = self.map[key]
            node.value = value
            self.order.remove(node)
            self.order.add_front(node)
            return
        if len(self.map) == self.capacity:
            victim = self.order.pop_back()   # back of list = least recently used
            del self.map[victim.key]
        node = _Node(key, value)
        self.map[key] = node
        self.order.add_front(node)


# ---- demo + self-checks ----------------------------------------------------
cache = LRUCache(2)
cache.put("a", 1)
cache.put("b", 2)
assert cache.get("a") == 1        # touches "a" -> "b" is now the LRU entry
cache.put("c", 3)                 # over capacity -> evicts "b", not "a"
assert cache.get("b") is None
assert cache.get("a") == 1 and cache.get("c") == 3
cache.put("a", 99)                # updating an existing key must NOT evict
assert cache.get("a") == 99 and cache.get("c") == 3
assert len(cache.map) == 2
print("LRU OK")

sections.title: 7. Worked Design: BookMyShow (Seat Locking)
sections.content:
The movie-ticket system is a concurrency question wearing a booking-app costume. The whole interview is one scenario: two users click seat A2 in the same second, and payment takes ninety seconds. Whoever models the gap between "I picked the seat" and "I paid for it" wins the round.

Requirements to lock in:
- A show has seats; a seat is AVAILABLE or BOOKED.
- Selecting seats gives the user an exclusive hold while they pay.
- The hold expires automatically (say 5 minutes) if payment never completes — otherwise abandoned carts freeze the seat map forever.
- Multi-seat selection is all-or-nothing: locking A1 but losing A2 must release A1, or the user owns a useless single seat and the map leaks locks.

The core mechanism is a TTL lock (time-to-live: the lock carries an expiry timestamp and is dead after it, no cleanup job required — expiry is checked lazily whenever someone asks). And a deliberate modelling choice: LOCKED is NOT a seat status. The Seat knows AVAILABLE or BOOKED; locks live in a SeatLockManager keyed by seat id. Why: if LOCKED were stored on the seat, an expired lock would leave a stale LOCKED seat needing a background sweeper to fix. With locks in the manager and expiry checked lazily, an expired lock is silently overwritable — no sweeper, no stale state, no 2 a.m. incident.

```
  BookingService                    SeatLockManager
  + hold(seats, user)      uses     - locks: {seat_id: SeatLock}
  + confirm(seats, user)  ----->    + lock(seat, user) -> bool
    (after payment)                 + holds_lock(seat, user)
                                    + release(seat)
                                          | creates
  Seat                                    v
  - status: AVAILABLE|BOOKED        SeatLock {user, expires_at}
                                    + is_expired(now)
              Clock (injected: now(), advance())
```

confirm() re-checks holds_lock for every seat before flipping anything to BOOKED — payment may have taken longer than the TTL, and confirming on a dead lock is exactly the double-booking the design exists to prevent. The injected Clock is what makes all of this assertable: the demo advances time past the TTL and proves the takeover works, with no sleep(301) in sight.

Probes to expect: "two app servers, so in-memory locks don't work" (move the manager's dict to Redis SET NX with EX for atomic lock-with-expiry, or a unique DB constraint on (show_id, seat_id) as the last line of defense), "payment succeeded but confirm found the lock expired" (payment goes through a reserve-then-capture flow, or you refund — name the compensating action), and "VIP seats need a longer TTL" (ttl becomes per-seat-category data passed to the manager — data change, not code change).

Thread-safety caveat (an interviewer WILL probe this): lock() is check-then-set, which is only atomic here because one in-process mutex serialises it. Across multiple servers a process mutex protects nothing — the real system moves the atomicity into the store (a Redis SET NX EX or a database unique constraint on seat_id+show_id), and the class becomes a client of that guarantee.

sections.title: 8. Worked Design: Notification Service (Strategy + Observer)
sections.content:
This question is a two-pattern exam, and the trap is believing Strategy and Observer are the same thing because both are "an interface with implementations". They solve different problems. Observer answers WHO gets told: something happened (an order shipped) and the publisher must not need to know who cares — coupling the order service to email code means every new reaction edits the order service. Strategy answers HOW one job is done: delivering this one message by email or SMS or push, chosen per user at runtime.

Requirements to lock in:
- Business events (order_shipped, payment_failed) fan out to interested parties.
- Each user has a preferred channel; channels will grow (push, WhatsApp) — open list, so Strategy.
- Adding a new consumer of events (an audit log, an analytics counter) must not touch the publisher.
- Delivery failure handling: out of scope today, but leave the seam visible (a retry decorator around a Channel).

```
  EventBus (subject)                    Observer (ABC)
  - subscribers: {event: [Observer]}        ^            ^
  + subscribe(event, obs)         NotificationService  AuditLog
  + publish(event, payload)             |
                                  uses  v  per user.preferred
                                  Channel (Strategy ABC)
                                      ^           ^
                                EmailChannel   SmsChannel
```

Follow one event through the system, out loud: OrderService calls bus.publish("order_shipped", payload) and returns — it knows nobody. The bus walks its subscriber list: NotificationService.on_event fires, looks up each user's preferred Channel by name, and calls send(); AuditLog.on_event appends a row. The proof that the shape is right: AuditLog was added by writing one class and one subscribe() call — the publisher and the notifier were not edited. That is the Open/Closed principle (open for extension, closed for modification) demonstrated rather than recited.

Two honest caveats earn points. Synchronous fan-out means a slow observer blocks the publisher — in production the bus hands events to a queue and observers consume asynchronously; say it, don't build it. And an observer that throws would kill the loop mid-fan-out — a real bus try/excepts per observer so one bad listener cannot starve the rest.

Probes to expect: "user wants email AND sms" (preference becomes a list; the loop sends to each — data shape change only), "add WhatsApp" (one new Channel class, zero edits — the Strategy payoff), "don't notify between 10pm and 8am" (a QuietHoursPolicy consulted by NotificationService — resist stuffing time logic into channels; delivery-time policy is not a delivery mechanism).

sections.title: 9. Worked Design: Rate Limiter (Token Bucket)
sections.content:
A rate limiter protects a service from any one client eating all capacity. The interview tests two things: do you know the standard algorithms and their trade-offs, and can you build one as clean classes with testable time handling — because naive rate limiters call time.time() deep inside, and then nobody can test them without actually waiting.

Requirements to lock in:
- Per-client limit, e.g. 3 requests burst, refilling 1 per second sustained.
- Bursts up to a cap are allowed (that requirement is what selects token bucket over leaky bucket).
- allow(client_id) -> bool, cheap enough to sit on the request path.
- Single process today; note where distributed state would go.

Why token bucket beats the alternatives here. A fixed window counter ("100 requests per minute, reset at :00") has the boundary burst: 100 requests at 11:59:59 and 100 more at 12:00:01 — 200 in two seconds, all allowed. Sliding window fixes that at the cost of more bookkeeping. Leaky bucket smooths output to a constant drip, which is wrong when the requirement explicitly permits bursts. Token bucket gives exactly the stated contract: capacity = maximum burst, refill rate = sustained average.

```
  RateLimiter (ABC)                       lazy refill, on demand:
       ^                                  elapsed = now - last
  TokenBucketLimiter                      tokens  = min(capacity,
  - buckets: {client_id: TokenBucket}         tokens + elapsed * rate)
  + allow(client_id) -> bool
       | has-many
       v
  TokenBucket {capacity, refill_per_sec, tokens, last}
  + try_consume() -> bool
       | uses
       v
  Clock (injected)
```

The elegant mechanism is LAZY refill: no background thread adds tokens every second. Each try_consume computes how much time passed since the last call and credits elapsed * rate tokens, capped at capacity. Same cost, no thread, no scheduling — and the cap is why a client idle for an hour still gets only a burst of 3, not 3600 stored-up requests.

The class split mirrors the parking lot: TokenBucket is one client's budget and knows nothing about clients; TokenBucketLimiter maps client ids to buckets and knows nothing about token math. Swap in a SlidingWindowLog class behind the same RateLimiter ABC and the limiter class does not change. Probes to expect: "different limits per API tier" (a config lookup chooses capacity/rate per client at bucket creation — data, not code), "multiple servers" (buckets move to Redis; the read-modify-write must be atomic, so a Lua script or token math via INCR — name the race, that is the point of the probe), and "thread safety" (one lock per bucket, not one global lock — unrelated clients should not queue behind each other).
sections.code:
"""Token bucket: a per-client counter that refills at a steady rate and
caps at a maximum (the burst size). Refill is computed lazily from
timestamps -- no background thread. Clock is injected for testability.
"""
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class Clock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.t = 0.0

    def now(self):
        return self.t

    def advance(self, secs):
        self.t += secs


class RateLimiter(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def allow(self, client_id: str) -> bool: ...


class TokenBucket:
    """One client's budget. capacity = max burst; refill_per_sec = long-run
    average rate the client is allowed to sustain."""
    def __init__(self, capacity: int, refill_per_sec: float, clock: Clock):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.refill_per_sec = refill_per_sec
        self.clock = clock
        self.tokens = float(capacity)        # start full: allow a first burst
        self.last = clock.now()

    def _refill(self):
        elapsed = self.clock.now() - self.last
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity,
                          self.tokens + elapsed * self.refill_per_sec)
        self.last = self.clock.now()

    def try_consume(self) -> bool:
        self._refill()
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False


class TokenBucketLimiter(RateLimiter):
    """Per-client buckets created lazily. Swap TokenBucket for a sliding-window
    class and THIS class does not change -- that is the extensibility seam."""
    def __init__(self, capacity: int, refill_per_sec: float, clock: Clock):
        self.capacity, self.rate, self.clock = capacity, refill_per_sec, clock
        self.buckets = {}                    # client_id -> TokenBucket

    def allow(self, client_id: str) -> bool:
        bucket = self.buckets.setdefault(
            client_id, TokenBucket(self.capacity, self.rate, self.clock))
        return bucket.try_consume()


# ---- demo + self-checks ----------------------------------------------------
clock = Clock()
limiter = TokenBucketLimiter(capacity=3, refill_per_sec=1.0, clock=clock)

burst = [limiter.allow("asha") for _ in range(5)]
assert burst == [True, True, True, False, False]   # burst of 3, then throttled
assert limiter.allow("bala")                       # separate bucket per client

clock.advance(2.0)                                 # 2 seconds -> 2 new tokens
assert limiter.allow("asha") and limiter.allow("asha")
assert not limiter.allow("asha")                   # both spent again

clock.advance(100.0)                               # long idle: refill CAPS at 3
assert [limiter.allow("asha") for _ in range(4)] == [True, True, True, False]
print("rate limiter OK")

sections.title: 10. Worked Design: Snake & Ladder (Board Game Modelling)
sections.content:
Board games look childish next to BookMyShow, which is exactly why interviewers use them: with zero domain difficulty, nothing hides your modelling. Every weakness — rules smeared across classes, untestable randomness, validation nowhere — is in plain sight. (Chess is the same interview with a bigger rulebook: Piece subclasses each owning their legal-move generation. Snake & Ladder fits in the time budget, so it is the one worked here.)

Requirements to lock in:
- Board of N cells (say 100); players start off-board at 0; first to land EXACTLY on N wins.
- Overshoot rule: if the roll goes past N, the player stays — confirm this, some house rules bounce back instead.
- Snakes move you down (head to tail), ladders move you up; at most one jump starts per cell; ignore chained jumps unless asked.
- Dice is 1..6 — but the DESIGN must let tests control the rolls.

```
  Game                              Dice
  - board, dice, players            + roll()
  + play_turn(player)                  ^ is-a
  + play() -> winner              LoadedDice(rolls)   <- tests inject this
       | has-a
       v
  Board                             Jump {start, end}
  - size                               ^           ^
  - jumps: {cell: cell}             Snake        Ladder
  + next_position(pos, roll)        (validates   (validates
                                     DOWN)        UP)
  Player {name, pos}
```

Three modelling decisions carry it. First, Board.next_position(pos, roll) is the single home of ALL movement rules — overshoot, snakes, ladders. Game never computes a position; it asks the board. When the interviewer adds a rule, you both already know which method changes. Second, Snake and Ladder subclass Jump and VALIDATE their direction in the constructor — an upward snake is rejected at construction time, not discovered mid-game three turns later. Making illegal objects unconstructible is cheap and reads as maturity. Third, Dice is injected into Game, and LoadedDice (a subclass returning a scripted sequence) makes the whole game deterministic: the demo asserts the exact winner. Say the phrase "I'm injecting the dice so my test is deterministic" — this is dependency injection (passing a class its collaborators from outside instead of letting it build its own) earning its keep in ten seconds.

Probes to expect: "roll a 6 grants another turn" (turn-advancing lives in Game.play — one method), "four players, configurable board" (already free: players is a list, size is a parameter — point that out), and "make it Chess" (Board becomes 2-D, Jump thinking becomes Piece.legal_moves(board) per subclass — the shape of the answer, one class per rule-owner, is the same).

sections.title: 11. Talking While Coding, and Surviving the 'Now Add X' Probe
sections.content:
Half your LLD grade comes from words, not code. The interviewer cannot read your mind; if you type in silence, they see keystrokes. But narrating syntax ("now I write a for loop") is noise. The rule: narrate DECISIONS and TRADE-OFFS, stay silent about mechanics.

The sentence pattern that carries the round has three parts — decision, reason, alternative: "I'm making pricing a separate strategy object, because you said hourly pricing 'for now', which tells me it changes; the alternative is a method on ParkingLot, and then every pricing change edits the lot class." One sentence like that per class is enough. Other high-value sentences: name the invariant when you create state ("net balances always sum to zero — I'll assert that"), name the deferral when you skip something ("I'm skipping input validation to get the flow working; flagging it so we can return"), and name what you are NOT building ("floors is a list, so multi-floor is free — I won't demo it").

The "now add X" probe is the most predictable moment of the interview, and most candidates still fumble it. When it comes, do not touch the keyboard. Answer in this exact shape:

```
1. WHERE  -> point at the seam: "that lands in PricingStrategy"
2. WHAT   -> the new code: "one new class, WeekendPricing"
3. UNTOUCHED -> "ParkingLot, Spot, Ticket don't change"
4. honest cost -> "if you ALSO want per-floor rates, the
                  strategy needs the floor -- interface gains a param"
```

Step 3 is the one candidates skip and the one that scores: LLD extensibility is measured in classes NOT edited. Step 4 matters because pretending every change is free reads as inexperience — a probe that genuinely breaks your interface ("now tickets are per-gate and gates go offline") deserves "that breaks my assumption that tickets live in one map; here is what I'd restructure", said calmly. Interviewers deliberately keep one probe that your design cannot absorb, to see whether you defend the design honestly or bluff.

Two rescue moves for when things go wrong. If you realize a class is bloating mid-flight, say it before they do: "ParkingLot is starting to do two jobs; I'd extract SpotAllocator — noting it and moving on for time." Naming your own smell converts a deduction into a point. If you blank on a pattern name, describe the mechanism instead — "I'll pass in an object that decides the fee, so implementations can vary" IS Strategy, and describing it without the label still passes; reciting the label without the mechanism does not.

sections.title: 12. The SOLID Smells Interviewers Hunt
sections.content:
Interviewers rarely ask "recite SOLID". They watch your code for five specific smells, each one letter, and probe the ones they see. Learn the smells, not the slogans.

```
S : class description needs "and"          -> god class
O : if/elif chain on a type string         -> closed for extension
L : subclass throws "not supported"        -> broken substitution
I : interface forces unused methods        -> fat interface
D : class builds its own dependencies      -> untestable, unswappable
```

S — Single Responsibility. The test is one sentence: "ParkingLot finds spots AND computes fees AND processes payments" — every "and" is a class trying to get out. The smell in code is a 200-line class other classes only partially use. The fix is extraction, and section 11 gave you the recovery script when you catch yourself live.

O — Open/Closed. The smell is `if type == "car": ... elif type == "truck": ...` repeated in three places; adding a bus means finding every chain, and missing one is a silent bug. The fix is polymorphism (each subclass carries its own behavior) or a strategy/dict lookup. Nuance worth saying: ONE dispatch point that builds the right object is fine — the smell is the chain COPIED across methods.

L — Liskov Substitution: any code holding a Vehicle must work when handed a Truck. The interview-classic bait is "add a CashPayment channel to your notification service" or square-extends-rectangle; the smell is a subclass whose method raises "not supported" or silently no-ops. If a subclass cannot honor the parent's contract, it is not a subclass — restructure (a Bird base class should not promise fly() if Penguin is coming; put fly() in a FlyingBird branch or a separate capability interface).

I — Interface Segregation. A fat Machine interface with print/scan/fax forces the cheap printer to stub fax(). Prefer several one-method interfaces — which is also why the Channel ABC in section 8 has exactly send() and nothing else.

D — Dependency Inversion. The smell is construction inside business logic: ParkingLot calling HourlyPricing() itself, a rate limiter calling time.time() directly, a game rolling random.randint inline. Every worked design here injected the variable part — pricing, Clock, Dice — which is why every demo could assert exact outcomes. When the interviewer asks "how would you test this?", a design with injected dependencies answers itself; a design without them has no good answer, and both of you will know.

Final calibration: patterns and principles are seasoning, not the meal. A design with three classes, one strategy, and honest trade-off talk beats one with six patterns and a Singleton nobody asked for. The interviewer is hiring a colleague, not a pattern catalog.

interviewQA.q: The interviewer says 'design a parking lot' and then stays silent. What do you do in the first five minutes?
interviewQA.a: Ask requirements questions and write the answers down where both of you can see them — the silence is the test, because the prompt is deliberately underspecified. Good questions for a parking lot: which vehicle types and can a small vehicle take a big spot; one floor or many; how is the fee computed (hourly? flat? per spot size?); what happens when the lot is full (refuse or queue?); do we need payments or does the round stop at the fee number. Four to six questions, then say the scope back: 'so: three vehicle types, best-fit spots, hourly pricing per spot size, refuse when full — I'll design for that.' Two payoffs: mid-round changes land in seams you planned, and at minute 25 you can point at the written bullet ('you said hourly for now') to justify why pricing is a swappable strategy. Coding before scoping is the single most common LLD fail.
followUps: What if the interviewer answers every question with 'up to you'?
How do you decide which requirements to explicitly declare out of scope?

interviewQA.q: In your parking lot, why is pricing a separate PricingStrategy class instead of a method on ParkingLot?
interviewQA.a: Because pricing is a variation point and ParkingLot is not. The requirement said 'hourly rates, per spot size — for now'; that 'for now' announces weekend rates, member discounts, surge pricing. If fee logic is a method on ParkingLot, every one of those changes edits the lot class, and the lot class is also the code that allocates spots and tracks tickets — so every pricing change risks breaking parking. As an injected Strategy (an object handed to ParkingLot that owns one decision: ticket in, fee out), each new scheme is a new class, tested alone, with zero edits to existing code. That is the Open/Closed principle doing real work rather than being recited. The honest counterweight: if pricing were genuinely fixed forever, the strategy would be ceremony — one interface, one implementation, no benefit. You add the seam because the requirement signaled change, and you should say exactly that reasoning out loud.
followUps: Now add weekend pricing that also depends on the floor — what changes?
When would introducing a Strategy be over-engineering?

interviewQA.q: Should vehicle types be subclasses (Car, Truck) or an enum field on one Vehicle class?
interviewQA.a: Decide by what varies: if the types differ only in DATA (a size, a rate key), an enum field is enough and subclasses are ceremony; if they differ in BEHAVIOR (different methods or rules per type), subclass so the behavior lives with the type instead of in if/elif chains. The parking lot sits at the boundary — Motorcycle/Car/Truck differ only in their minimum spot size, so a pure enum design is defensible, and saying so earns points for judgment. Subclassing still wins slightly here because the interview's next probes ('add an EV that needs charging', 'trucks pay a surcharge') add behavior, and with subclasses each probe is a new class rather than a new branch in every method that switches on the enum. The failure mode to avoid is the worst of both: an enum PLUS scattered if vehicle.type == CAR chains — that is the Open/Closed smell interviewers hunt. State the rule, pick one, and name what would make you switch.
followUps: The lot now needs EV spots with chargers — enum value or new class, and why?
How does this same decision show up in the Splitwise split modes?

interviewQA.q: How do you model an elevator so it does not become a pile of booleans?
interviewQA.a: Make the mode a single enum-valued state field — IDLE, MOVING_UP, MOVING_DOWN, DOOR_OPEN — and put every legal transition in one step() method that fires once per tick. The boolean pile (is_moving, going_up, doors_open) allows nonsense like moving with doors open, and every method must defensively re-check combinations; with one enum, invalid states are unrepresentable — the elevator IS exactly one thing. Concentrating transitions in step() makes the machine auditable: the interviewer reads one method and verifies the transition table is complete (IDLE goes to MOVING when targets exist; MOVING goes to DOOR_OPEN on arrival; DOOR_OPEN drains to MOVING or IDLE). The tick-based design also kills the threading temptation: a step() you call in a loop is deterministic and assertable, while a thread with sleeps cannot be tested in an interview. Keep dispatch (which car answers a hall call) in a separate ElevatorController so policy changes never touch the state machine.
followUps: Add an EMERGENCY_STOP state — walk me through exactly what changes.
Why does the controller choose the car instead of the elevator choosing its own calls?

interviewQA.q: Two idle elevators, a call comes from floor 6. Where does the choosing code live and how would you improve the policy?
interviewQA.a: It lives in ElevatorController.call(), not in Elevator — the split is physics versus policy. An elevator knows how to move itself one legal transition at a time; it should not know about its siblings or about dispatch fairness, because then every policy change edits the state machine. The controller holds the fleet and picks a car by a cost function: version one is nearest-car (min distance). The known weakness: nearest-car ignores direction — a car one floor above you but committed downward with five targets is 'nearest' and still a bad pick. Version two scores direction-aware cost: a car moving toward the caller costs its distance; a car moving away costs its remaining trip plus the return. Because policy is isolated, the upgrade is either an edit to one method or, cleaner, a DispatchPolicy strategy injected into the controller so nearest-car and direction-aware are two swappable classes. That last sentence is usually exactly what the probe was fishing for.
followUps: How would you avoid starving a top-floor call during heavy lobby traffic?
What changes if elevators serve disjoint floor ranges, like a service car?

interviewQA.q: Explain Splitwise's simplify-debts. Is the greedy result the true minimum number of payments?
interviewQA.a: First reduce everything to net balances: each expense adds the full amount to the payer's net and subtracts each participant's share, so sum(net) == 0 always — that invariant is your correctness assert. Simplification then ignores WHO paid WHOM historically; only nets matter. Greedy: sort debtors most-negative first, creditors most-positive first, and repeatedly have the biggest debtor pay the biggest creditor min(|debt|, credit). Each payment zeroes at least one person, so n people with nonzero balances settle in at most n-1 transfers. But no — that is a bound, not the minimum. The true minimum is NP-hard because it hides subset-sum: if some subgroup's balances cancel exactly (say +700 against -400 and -300), settling that subgroup internally saves a transfer, and finding such subsets is the hard part. For a friend group of 5, greedy's n-1 is what the real product ships; say the caveat before the interviewer springs it and the question is fully defused.
followUps: Why must the balances be integer paise instead of floats?
Equal split of 100 paise among 3 people — where does the extra paisa go and why must shares sum exactly?

interviewQA.q: Why does an LRU cache need both a hashmap AND a doubly linked list?
interviewQA.a: Because get and put must both be O(1), and each structure alone answers only half the problem. A hashmap finds the node for a key in O(1) but has no usable notion of 'oldest' — finding the least recently used key would be an O(n) scan. A list keeps recency order but finding a given key inside it is O(n). Combined: map from key to node gives O(1) lookup; the doubly linked list holds nodes in recency order so move-to-front on every touch and evict-from-back on overflow are both O(1) pointer operations. Doubly linked specifically because removing a node from the middle requires rewiring its predecessor, and only a doubly linked node knows its predecessor without an O(n) walk. The design point on top of the DSA: cage the pointer surgery in a _DoublyLinkedList class with three verbs (add_front, remove, pop_back) plus sentinel end nodes so there are no empty-list special cases, and let LRUCache read like policy: on get, move to front; on overflow, pop back.
followUps: The interviewer says 'now make it LFU' — what is the honest answer about what changes?
Would Python's OrderedDict be an acceptable answer in this round?

interviewQA.q: Two users click the same BookMyShow seat in the same second. Walk me through what your design does.
interviewQA.a: Both clicks race to SeatLockManager.lock(seat, user). The manager holds one lock record per seat id; the first click finds no live lock and writes SeatLock(user=asha, expires_at=now+300). The second click finds a live, unexpired lock owned by someone else and returns False immediately — Bala's UI shows the seat taken and offers alternatives. Asha now has five minutes to pay. If she pays, confirm() re-verifies she still holds every lock, flips the seats to BOOKED, and releases the locks. If she abandons, nothing happens at all: the lock simply expires, because expiry is a timestamp checked lazily on the next access — no cleanup job. When Bala retries at minute six, lock() sees the lock is expired and overwrites it. For multi-seat holds the service is all-or-nothing: fail on seat 3 of 3 and it releases seats 1 and 2, otherwise the seat map leaks partial holds. In one process this is a dict; the same protocol maps onto Redis SET NX EX when there are many app servers.
followUps: Why is LOCKED deliberately not a value of SeatStatus?
Payment succeeded at second 310 but the TTL was 300 — what happens and how do you fix the flow?

interviewQA.q: Why lock seats with a TTL instead of holding the lock until the user finishes or cancels?
interviewQA.a: Because on the web, 'cancel' mostly never arrives. Users close tabs, phones die, payments hang at a gateway — with an unlimited hold, every abandoned cart freezes a seat until an admin or a batch job frees it, and popular shows bleed sellable inventory all evening. A TTL (time-to-live: the lock stores expires_at and is considered dead after it) makes abandonment self-healing with zero infrastructure: no cleanup daemon, no cancel webhook dependency — the next lock attempt checks the timestamp lazily and overwrites a dead lock. The TTL value is a product trade-off you should name: too short and slow payers lose seats mid-payment; too long and abandoned seats stay dark; ~5 minutes matches a payment flow. The same reasoning rejects holding a DB transaction open during payment: a transaction pinned for minutes holds row locks and a connection hostage, and a gateway timeout turns into database pressure. Short-lived application locks plus a final atomic re-check at confirm time is the standard shape.
followUps: What guards double-booking if the app-server lock layer itself crashes?
Where does the compensating action live when payment succeeds after the lock expired?

interviewQA.q: You used both Strategy and Observer in the notification service. Aren't they the same thing — an interface with implementations?
interviewQA.a: Mechanically they rhyme — both are polymorphism through an interface — but they solve opposite problems, and the interviewer asks this to check you know patterns by problem, not by shape. Observer decouples an event SOURCE from its CONSUMERS: the order service publishes 'order_shipped' to a bus and returns, knowing nobody; notifier, audit log, analytics each subscribe independently, and adding a consumer touches zero existing code. It is one-to-many, and the set of listeners changes at runtime. Strategy decouples a JOB from its METHOD: delivering this one message by email versus SMS is one slot filled by one interchangeable object, chosen per user. It is one-to-one at the call site. The memory hook: Observer = WHO reacts when something happens; Strategy = HOW one thing gets done. In this design they compose — the NotificationService is an Observer of the bus, and inside its on_event it selects a Channel Strategy per user preference. Being able to point at both roles in your own code is the strong answer.
followUps: What breaks if a slow or throwing observer sits in the synchronous fan-out loop?
A user now wants email AND sms — which pattern's side changes, and how?

interviewQA.q: Compare token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, and sliding window. Why pick token bucket?
interviewQA.a: Fixed window counts requests per clock window ('100/minute, reset at :00') — cheapest, but has the boundary burst: 100 requests at 11:59:59 plus 100 at 12:00:01 is 200 in two seconds, all allowed. Sliding window (log or weighted approximation) fixes the boundary by measuring the trailing 60 seconds, at the cost of storing timestamps or interpolating two counters. Leaky bucket queues arrivals and drains at a constant rate — output is perfectly smooth, which is right for shaping traffic TO a fragile downstream but wrong when clients are promised bursts. Token bucket: tokens drip in at the sustained rate, pool up to capacity, and each request spends one — so capacity IS the burst allowance and refill rate IS the long-run average, which directly encodes the usual API contract 'burst of N, sustained R/sec'. Implementation is two floats per client with lazy refill (tokens = min(cap, tokens + elapsed*rate) computed on each request — no background thread). Pick by requirement, and say which requirement: bursts allowed means token bucket; smooth output means leaky; approximate fairness at minimal memory means sliding window counter.
followUps: Why does lazy refill need the min(capacity, ...) cap — what breaks without it?
Your limiter must now run on 5 app servers — what becomes the hard part?

interviewQA.q: Why do your rate limiter and booking service take a Clock object instead of calling time.time()?
interviewQA.a: Because time.time() buried inside a class makes its behavior a function of wall-clock reality, and then the only way to test 'lock expires after 300 seconds' is to actually wait 300 seconds — so nobody tests it, and expiry bugs ship. Injecting a Clock (an object with now(), handed in at construction) is dependency injection: the class declares 'I depend on time' in its signature, and the test hands it a FakeClock with an advance() method. The demo then proves TTL takeover and token refill with exact asserts in microseconds, deterministically — no flaky sleeps. Production passes a real clock; nothing else changes. The identical move appears as LoadedDice in Snake & Ladder: randomness, like time, is an ambient dependency that destroys determinism unless you inject it. This is the Dependency Inversion principle in its most practical form, and it is why 'how would you test this?' is a question my design answers by construction — which is precisely what that interview question is probing for.
followUps: What other ambient dependencies deserve the same treatment in an LLD round?
Is injecting a Clock over-engineering for production code that only ever uses real time?

interviewQA.q: The interviewer says: 'make your LRU cache thread-safe.' What is the strong answer?
interviewQA.a: Start by naming the race precisely: two threads calling put() at capacity can both run the evict-then-insert sequence and corrupt the linked list — pointer surgery is multi-step, so a context switch mid-rewire leaves the list broken. First fix: one lock (a mutex — mutual exclusion object only one thread can hold) around the bodies of get and put. Say explicitly that this is the RIGHT first answer, not a naive one: the critical sections are a handful of pointer moves, so contention is cheap, and a coarse lock is provably correct. Note the subtlety that get also mutates (move-to-front), so readers need the lock too — a reader/writer split does not apply cleanly to LRU. Only if the interviewer pushes on contention: shard the keyspace into K independent LRUCache instances each with its own lock (hash(key) % K picks the shard), trading exact global LRU order for K-way parallelism — which is what production caches actually do. Offering correct-then-scalable, in that order and labeled as such, is the maturity signal this probe exists to detect.
followUps: Why can't you make get() lock-free by skipping the move-to-front?
What does Python's GIL change about this answer, if anything?

interviewQA.q: When do you choose composition over inheritance, and where did that choice show up in these designs?
interviewQA.a: The test is substitutability, not vocabulary convenience: use inheritance only when the subclass IS a drop-in variant of the parent — every caller holding the parent type must work unchanged when handed the child (that is Liskov). Use composition (the class HOLDS a collaborator and delegates) for capabilities, policies, and anything that varies independently. The tell for wrong inheritance is a subclass overriding a method to raise 'not supported', or a hierarchy trying to encode two independent axes at once — SmallElectricCar, LargeElectricCar, SmallPetrolCar... the combinatorial explosion means those axes wanted to be two composed fields, not one tree. In these designs, inheritance appears exactly where variants are substitutable: Car/Truck under Vehicle, LoadedDice under Dice, EmailChannel under Channel. Composition carries everything else: ParkingLot HAS floors and HAS a pricing strategy; Game HAS a board and a dice; BookingService HAS a lock manager. Rule of thumb worth saying aloud: inheritance for the interface's implementations, composition for the object graph.
followUps: Your Vehicle hierarchy now needs electric variants of every type — restructure it.
Why is LoadedDice extending Dice safe by the Liskov test?

interviewQA.q: What is a god class, and how do you notice you are writing one mid-interview?
interviewQA.a: A god class is one class that hoards the whole system's knowledge and behavior — the 400-line ParkingLot that stores spots, picks them, prices tickets, processes payments, and prints receipts. It is the number-one LLD failure because it makes every future change touch the same file and makes nothing testable in isolation; interviewers spot it instantly and probe until it hurts. Live detection signals: describing the class needs 'and' ('it finds spots AND computes fees'); methods clustering into groups that never touch each other's fields (two classes cohabiting); every new requirement landing in the same class; the class name drifting toward Manager, Handler, or the system's own name. The recovery move scores points rather than losing them, but only if YOU say it first: 'ParkingLot is accumulating a second job — spot allocation wants to be its own SpotAllocator; I'll note the split and keep moving for time.' Naming your own smell demonstrates the exact code-review judgment the round is buying. Waiting for the interviewer to point at it demonstrates the opposite.
followUps: Is a thin coordinator class that only delegates also a smell?
How small is too small — when does splitting classes become noise?

interviewQA.q: The interviewer says 'now add X' — say, EV charging spots to your parking lot. What are they testing and what is the ideal response shape?
interviewQA.a: They are testing whether your earlier structure was real. The probe is scripted before you wrote a line, and it measures one number: how many EXISTING classes must change to absorb X. The response shape, before touching the keyboard: WHERE — point at the seam ('spot types live in SpotSize plus ParkingSpot; charging is a capability of a spot'); WHAT — the new code ('an EV_COMPACT size or a chargeable flag, a ChargingSpot subclass if charging has behavior like billing kWh'); UNTOUCHED — the list of classes that do not change ('ParkingLot, Ticket, the pricing interface stand'); and the honest cost — what genuinely gets harder ('if charging is billed per kWh, PricingStrategy.fee needs energy data on the ticket — that is an interface change and I would version it'). The UNTOUCHED list is the scoring line almost everyone forgets. And when a probe truly breaks your design, say so calmly and restructure — interviewers usually hold one deliberately breaking probe to see whether you bluff. Defending honestly beats pretending elasticity you do not have.
followUps: Give an example of a probe that SHOULD break the parking lot design as coded.
How do you buy time gracefully when you cannot immediately see the seam?

interviewQA.q: How much SOLID vocabulary should you actually say out loud in the round?
interviewQA.a: Use the mechanism always, the label at most once each, and never a label without pointing at the line of code earning it. Interviewers are pattern-matched against buzzword recitation — 'I follow SOLID principles' scores zero and invites a probe you may not survive. What scores: demonstrations attached to decisions. 'Each split mode is its own class, so percentage split is an add, not an edit' IS Open/Closed, and appending '...which is the open/closed idea' costs three words and lands fine. 'I'm injecting the clock so tests control time' IS dependency inversion. 'This subclass would have to throw on that inherited method, so it should not be a subclass' IS Liskov. If you blank on a name, describe the mechanism and keep moving — a described mechanism without its label passes; a label without its mechanism fails, because the follow-up ('show me where') has nowhere to land. Same rule for design patterns: say Strategy or Observer when you build one, at the moment you build it, tied to the problem it solves — 'the publisher must not know its listeners, so: observer.'
followUps: The interviewer asks you to define a principle you used implicitly — how do you structure that answer?
Which SOLID letter is most often faked by candidates, in your view, and how do interviewers catch it?

interviewQA.q: Design-wise, what is the difference between modelling Snake & Ladder and modelling Chess, and what stays the same?
interviewQA.a: The rulebook grows but the modelling shape is identical, which is why either works as the board-game question. Snake & Ladder concentrates ALL movement law in Board.next_position — overshoot, snakes, ladders — because rules are position-triggered and piece-independent; players are dumb tokens. Chess inverts the ownership: rules are PIECE-dependent, so each Piece subclass owns its legal-move generation (Knight.legal_moves(board), Pawn with its direction, capture, and promotion quirks), the 2-D Board owns occupancy and bounds, and a Game/Referee layer owns cross-cutting law that no single piece can know — check (is my king attacked after this move?), castling rights, turn order. What stays the same across both: every rule has exactly one home class, so any rule change has one obvious landing spot; the random or interactive input is injected (LoadedDice, a scripted MovePlayer) so games are deterministic under test; and illegal states are rejected at construction (an upward snake, a ninth rank). If asked to switch mid-round, say the mapping in one line — 'Jump-rules-in-Board becomes legal-moves-in-Piece' — and the interviewer hears transferable design, not memorized solutions.
followUps: In Chess, why can't Piece.legal_moves alone decide legality — what needs the Game layer?
Add the 'roll a 6 goes again' rule — which single method changes and why is it Game, not Board?

flashcards.front: LLD vs HLD vs DSA round — one line each?
flashcards.back: DSA: one function, graded on correctness + complexity. LLD: 5-10 classes in one process, graded on decomposition + extensibility. HLD: many machines, graded on scaling trade-offs.

flashcards.front: The 4-step LLD method and its 45-minute budget?
flashcards.back: 1) Requirements ~5 min (ask + write bullets). 2) Entities ~10 (nouns->classes, verbs->methods). 3) Relationships ~5 (is-a/has-a, interfaces at variation points). 4) Code ONE flow end to end ~20. Keep ~5 min for the 'now add X' probe.

flashcards.front: Why ask requirements first when the prompt is one vague line?
flashcards.back: The vagueness IS the test: they check you extract scope before coding. Written bullets also become ammunition — 'you said hourly for now' justifies the pricing strategy seam at minute 25.

flashcards.front: What is a god class and its fastest detection test?
flashcards.back: One class hoarding the system's knowledge and behavior (ParkingLot that stores, allocates, prices, pays). Test: describe the class in one sentence — every 'and' is a class trying to get out.

flashcards.front: Strategy pattern — the problem it solves, in one line?
flashcards.back: HOW one job gets done varies (pricing, split mode, delivery channel): put the decision behind an interface and inject an interchangeable object, so new variants are new classes, not edits.

flashcards.front: Observer pattern — the problem it solves, in one line?
flashcards.back: WHO reacts to an event must not be known to the publisher: it publishes to a bus; listeners subscribe independently. Adding a listener (audit log) touches zero existing code.

flashcards.front: Memory hook to keep Strategy and Observer apart?
flashcards.back: Observer = WHO gets told when something happens (one-to-many fan-out). Strategy = HOW one thing gets done (one slot, one interchangeable object). They compose: an observer can pick a strategy inside its handler.

flashcards.front: Why does an elevator get an enum state machine instead of booleans?
flashcards.back: Booleans (is_moving, doors_open) allow nonsense combos like moving with doors open. One enum state (IDLE/MOVING_UP/MOVING_DOWN/DOOR_OPEN) makes invalid states unrepresentable; all transitions live in one step() you can audit.

flashcards.front: Elevator design: what does Elevator own vs ElevatorController?
flashcards.back: Elevator owns physics: its state, targets, and step() with every legal transition. Controller owns policy: which car answers a hall call. Policy upgrades swap the controller; the state machine never changes.

flashcards.front: Parking lot: why BEST-FIT spot allocation instead of first free spot?
flashcards.back: Best fit = smallest free spot that fits. First-fit parks a car in the only LARGE spot, and the next truck is refused despite capacity existing. Best fit preserves big spots for vehicles that need them.

flashcards.front: Parking fee: charge by vehicle size or by spot size?
flashcards.back: By SPOT size: a car occupying a LARGE spot blocked large capacity, so it pays the LARGE rate. The price is for the capacity consumed, not for what the vehicle is.

flashcards.front: Splitwise ledger invariant to state and assert?
flashcards.back: sum of all net balances == 0, after every expense, forever. Payer's net += full amount; each participant's net -= their share. Any drift means a split leaked money.

flashcards.front: Equal split of 100 paise among 3 — handling the remainder?
flashcards.back: divmod(100,3) = 33 rem 1; the first `rem` participants absorb one extra paisa (34+33+33). Shares must sum EXACTLY to the amount — and money is integer paise, never floats.

flashcards.front: Splitwise simplify: the greedy algorithm and its bound?
flashcards.back: Sort debtors most-negative, creditors most-positive; biggest debtor pays biggest creditor min(|debt|, credit); repeat. Each payment zeroes someone, so at most n-1 transfers for n nonzero balances.

flashcards.front: Is Splitwise's minimum-transfers problem solvable optimally?
flashcards.back: Finding the true minimum is NP-hard — it hides subset-sum (subgroups whose balances cancel exactly save a transfer). Greedy's n-1 bound is what the real product ships; say the caveat unprompted.

flashcards.front: LRU cache: why a hashmap AND a doubly linked list?
flashcards.back: Hashmap: O(1) key->node lookup but no notion of oldest. DLL: O(1) move-to-front and evict-from-back but O(n) key search. Together both get and put are O(1).

flashcards.front: LRU: why DOUBLY linked, not singly?
flashcards.back: Removing a middle node needs its predecessor rewired in O(1); only a doubly linked node knows its prev without an O(n) walk from the head.

flashcards.front: LRU: what do sentinel head/tail nodes buy you?
flashcards.back: Permanent dummy end nodes mean add_front/remove/pop_back never special-case an empty list or first/last element — about four if-branches (and their bugs) deleted.

flashcards.front: LRU as class design: where may pointer surgery appear?
flashcards.back: Only inside _DoublyLinkedList (add_front, remove, pop_back). LRUCache reads as policy: on get, move node to front; on overflow, pop back + delete from map. Cache code touching prev/next = leaked abstraction.

flashcards.front: The classic LRU bug interviewers watch for?
flashcards.back: get() that returns the value without moving the node to the front — recency never updates, so the wrong key gets evicted. Also: put() on an EXISTING key must update + refresh, never evict.

flashcards.front: BookMyShow: why is LOCKED not a SeatStatus value?
flashcards.back: A LOCKED status on the seat goes stale when the lock expires, needing a cleanup sweeper. Keep locks in SeatLockManager with expires_at, checked lazily: an expired lock is silently overwritten. Seat stays AVAILABLE/BOOKED only.

flashcards.front: Why do seat locks carry a TTL?
flashcards.back: Web users abandon carts without cancelling; an unlimited hold freezes seats forever. TTL makes abandonment self-healing with no cleanup job — the next lock attempt sees the dead timestamp and overwrites. ~5 min matches a payment flow.

flashcards.front: Multi-seat hold rule in a booking system?
flashcards.back: All-or-nothing: if seat 3 of 3 fails to lock, release seats 1 and 2 before returning failure. Otherwise the user holds useless partial seats and the seat map leaks locks.

flashcards.front: Why must confirm() re-check locks before marking seats BOOKED?
flashcards.back: Payment can outlive the TTL. If the lock expired (and maybe someone else took the seat), confirming blindly double-books. Re-verify holds_lock per seat; on failure, refund/compensate instead.

flashcards.front: Token bucket: what do capacity and refill rate encode?
flashcards.back: capacity = maximum burst allowed at once; refill_per_sec = sustained long-run average rate. Together they state the usual API contract directly: 'burst of N, R per second sustained'.

flashcards.front: Token bucket lazy refill — formula and why no thread?
flashcards.back: On each request: tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed*rate); last = now. Computing refill from timestamps on demand equals a background thread's effect with zero threads — and min(cap,...) stops an idle hour becoming 3600 stored requests.

flashcards.front: Fixed window counter's boundary-burst flaw?
flashcards.back: '100/min resetting at :00' allows 100 requests at 11:59:59 and 100 more at 12:00:01 — 200 in two seconds. Sliding windows or token bucket fix it.

flashcards.front: Token bucket vs leaky bucket — pick by which requirement?
flashcards.back: Bursts permitted up to a cap -> token bucket (tokens pool). Output must be perfectly smooth for a fragile downstream -> leaky bucket (queue drains at constant rate).

flashcards.front: Dependency injection — definition and its interview payoff?
flashcards.back: Pass a class its collaborators (Clock, Dice, PricingStrategy) from outside instead of letting it construct its own. Tests then substitute fakes: FakeClock.advance() proves TTL expiry, LoadedDice makes a game deterministic — no sleeps, no flakes.

flashcards.front: Composition vs inheritance — the deciding test?
flashcards.back: Inheritance only if the child is a substitutable drop-in for the parent everywhere (Liskov). Capabilities and policies that vary independently = composition. Two independent axes in one tree (SmallElectricCar...) = explosion; make them composed fields.

flashcards.front: Liskov violation — the smell in code?
flashcards.back: A subclass overriding an inherited method to raise 'not supported' or silently no-op. If the child can't honor the parent's contract it isn't a subclass — restructure (capability interface or a separate branch).

flashcards.front: Open/Closed smell interviewers hunt in LLD code?
flashcards.back: The same if/elif chain on a type string copied across methods — adding a type means finding every chain. Fix: polymorphism or a strategy/dict lookup. One single dispatch point that builds the right object is fine.

flashcards.front: Answer shape for the 'now add X' probe?
flashcards.back: Before typing: WHERE (point at the seam), WHAT (the new class), UNTOUCHED (list classes that don't change — the scoring line), honest COST (what genuinely gets harder). If it truly breaks the design, say so and restructure calmly.

flashcards.front: What should you narrate while coding in an LLD round?
flashcards.back: Decisions and trade-offs, not syntax: 'strategy here because pricing was said to change; alternative was a method on the lot.' Also name invariants ('nets sum to zero'), and deferrals ('skipping validation, flagging it').

flashcards.front: Snake & Ladder: which class owns ALL movement rules and why?
flashcards.back: Board.next_position(pos, roll) — overshoot, snakes, ladders in one method. Game only loops turns. Every rule having exactly one home means every rule change has one obvious landing spot.

flashcards.front: Why are Snake and Ladder constructor-validated subclasses of Jump?
flashcards.back: Snake asserts tail < head, Ladder asserts top > bottom: an illegal jump is rejected at construction, not discovered mid-game turns later. Making invalid objects unconstructible is cheap maturity signal.

flashcards.front: Enum field vs subclass for a 'type' — the deciding question?
flashcards.back: Does the type vary only in DATA (size, rate key) -> enum field. Does it vary in BEHAVIOR (per-type rules/methods) -> subclass, so behavior lives with the type instead of in scattered if/elif chains.
